signals.title: [ROCm] Enable safe AITER MoE dispatch for Qwen3.6 on gfx12
signals.text: ## Purpose Enable safe Qwen3.6 BF16 AITER MoE serving on gfx12/RDNA4. Currently, enabling AITER MoE for this model family can route serving traffic into unsupported AITER runtime shapes and fail with: ```text RuntimeError: wrong! device_gemm with the specified compilation parameters does not support this GEMM problem ``` This PR provides the vLLM-side bridge needed by the AITER enablement stack: - AITER issue: <https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/issues/4492> - AITER dependency: <https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/4385> - AITER PR1, small-token-count direct path: <https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/4740> - AITER PR2, Qwen3.6 gfx1201 tuning data: <https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/4815> - AITER PR3, M8/M16 direct path: <https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/4838> The main purpose is to preserve the AITER weight-layout contract across vLLM's custom-op boundary and to avoid hard failures when gfx12 BF16 G1U1 AITER reports an unsupported runtime shape. Supported shapes use AITER; unsupported gfx12 BF16 G1U1 shapes fall back to the existing vLLM Triton MoE path. ## Test Plan Kernel-level validation compares AITER against vLLM Triton MoE using the same Qwen3.6 BF16 weights, routing inputs, and token counts. - AITER PR1 path: `fused_moe -> fmoe_g1u1_bf16_small_m`, implemented in <https://github.com/keneoneth/aiter/blob/fix/gfx1201-bf16-g1u1-small-m-moe/aiter/fused_moe.py> and <https://github.com/keneoneth/aiter/blob/fix/gfx1201-bf16-g1u1-small-m-moe/csrc/py_itfs_cu/asm_fmoe.cu> - AITER PR3 path: `fused_moe -> m8_m16_direct_2stage`, implemented in <https://github.com/keneoneth/aiter/blob/feat/gfx1201-bf16-g1u1-m8-m16-direct-moe/aiter/ops/triton/moe_m8_m16_direct_2stage.py> - vLLM baseline path: `fused_experts`, implemented in <https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/fused_moe.py> Full GuideLLM serving comparison was run with this vLLM bridge plus the AITER PR1/PR2/PR3 stack: ```text model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B BF16 GPU: gfx1201 parallelism: TP2 / PP2 max_model_len: 16640 max_num_seqs: 240 prompt/output tokens: 2000 / 1000 GuideLLM sweep: 10 points, 1000 requests baseline env: VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1, VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_MOE=0 AITER MoE env: VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1, VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_MOE=1 ``` ## Test Result Kernel-level latency comparison: `M` is the number of tokens in the MoE batch. `inter_dim` is the per-expert intermediate dimension for the gated MLP. `Latency improvement vs vLLM` is `(vLLM mean us - AITER mean us) / vLLM mean us`. | AITER path | inter_dim | M | AITER mean us | vLLM mean us | Latency reduction (AITER vs vLLM) | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | PR1 direct small-token-count path | 128 | 1 | 92.826 | 162.170 | 42.8% | | PR1 direct small-token-count path | 128 | 2 | 102.977 | 159.899 | 35.6% | | PR1 direct small-token-count path | 128 | 3 | 118.921 | 161.082 | 26.2% | | PR1 direct small-token-count path | 128 | 4 | 131.988 | 161.309 | 18.2% | | PR1 direct small-token-count path | 256 | 1 | 112.105 | 161.805 | 30.7% | | PR1 direct small-token-count path | 256 | 2 | 133.689 | 163.170 | 18.1% | | PR1 direct small-token-count path | 256 | 3 | 196.396 | 204.827 | 4.1% | | PR1 direct small-token-count path | 256 | 4 | 263.561 | 304.124 | 13.3% | | PR3 direct M8/M16 path | 128 | 8 | 208.682 | 305.722 | 31.7% | | PR3 direct M8/M16 path | 128 | 16 | 351.489 | 470.975 | 25.4% | | PR3 direct M8/M16 path | 256 | 8 | 372.676 | 469.505 | 20.6% | | PR3 direct M8/M16 path | 256 | 16 | 644.113 | 765.884 | 15.9% | Full GuideLLM serving comparison: | Mode | Safe concurrency | Safe request rate | Request throughput | Output tok/s | TPOT ms | TTFT ms | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | vLLM Triton MoE baseline | 48 | 0.720 | 0.560 | 562.745 | 63.919 | 343.142 | | AITER MoE | 54 | 0.800 | 0.620 | 622.194 | 64.565 | 392.354 | | AITER MoE delta | +12.5% | +11.1% | +10.7% | +10.6% | -1.0% | -14.3% | This PR provides the vLLM-side safety bridge needed to enable Qwen3.6 BF16 AITER MoE on gfx12/RDNA4 without exposing serving to unsupported AITER runtime shapes. Supported gfx1201 BF16 G1U1 shapes now use the new AITER kernels, while unsupported shapes fall back to the existing vLLM Triton MoE path instead of failing with `wrong! device_gemm`. With the AITER PR1/PR2/PR3 stack, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B BF16 TP2/PP2 serving completes successfully with AITER MoE enabled. Targeted kernel tests show up to **42.8%** latency reduction on small-M decode shapes, and GuideLLM serving improves safe concurrency by **12.5%**, safe request rate by **11.1%**, request throughput by **10.7%**, and output token throughput by **10.6%**. --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [ ] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [ ] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [ ] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details> **BEFORE SUBMITTING, PLEASE READ <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/contributing>** (anything written below this line will be removed by GitHub Actions)

signals.title: [Bugfix][Spec Decode] DFlash2: accept unquantized linear LM heads in the candidate selector
signals.text: ## Purpose Stacked on **#52816** — this branch is `19c93519` plus one commit, so the diff above includes that PR's changes. Retarget to `main` once #52816 merges; the diff then collapses to the single fix commit. `DFlash2Qwen3ForCausalLM.compute_candidates` guards the LM head with `isinstance(self.lm_head.quant_method, UnquantizedEmbeddingMethod)`, but that class only appears when the model has no quant config at all. A quantization config that leaves the head unquantized — INC, ModelOpt, fp8 with excluded layers, ... — returns `UnquantizedLinearMethod` for a `ParallelLMHead` (the same class it returns for any unquantized linear). A quantized-body target with an unquantized head therefore fails to start: ``` ValueError: DFlash2 requires an unquantized target LM head for candidate TopK. ``` Reproduced with `z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B` (INC-int4, head unquantized) as target and `z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` as drafter, TP2 on dual RTX 3090. Both classes are unquantized and their `apply()` dispatches the same unquantized GEMM, so the guard now accepts either, and the error names the offending method. Also types the `config` parameter as `Qwen3Config` to match the base class signature. ## Why this is not a duplicate #52816 introduces the DFlash2 architecture; this PR only fixes the LM-head guard in the code that PR adds, on top of its head. No other open PR touches this path. ## Test plan - `ruff check` / `ruff format --check` on the touched file → clean. - Startup with the INC-int4 target above; drafts k=7, measure acceptance. - (to be filled with exact commands + results) ## Test Result (to be filled) ## Note AI assistance (pi coding agent) was used for the fix and this description; every changed line was reviewed and tested by the submitter.

signals.title: [Rust Frontend] Replace external `protoc` with pure Rust lib `protox`
signals.text: ## Purpose The Rust frontend currently requires an external `protoc` executable to generate its gRPC bindings. This adds a host-tool dependency to local builds, CI jobs, wheel builders, and Docker build stages. This PR: - compiles `control.proto` and `inference.proto` with the pure-Rust `protox` compiler and passes the resulting descriptor set to `tonic-prost-build`; - removes the obsolete `--experimental_allow_proto3_optional` argument; - removes the `protoc` installer and installation steps that were added specifically for the Rust frontend across Buildkite, macOS wheel builds, and Rust Docker stages. ## Purpose Extend the existing ROCm AITER `fuse_qk_norm_rope_kvcache` compile pass with a gated-QKV pattern. signals.title: [Bugfix][DP] Synchronize the device on pause completion
signals.text:
Addresses the third problem in #51476: `pause_generation()` resolves before the device is idle — and in DP, the pause path is itself what makes the device busy. Companion PR #52957 (independent, no shared commits) removes the DP dummy-batch burst; this PR makes the pause completion contract correct regardless of how much work is in flight. ## Purpose **1. Pause completion is a CPU-side predicate.** The pause future resolves off `has_work()` and the DP consensus is a gloo CPU all-reduce; nothing on the pause path touches a CUDA stream. `sleep()` is safe only because `GPUWorker.sleep` synchronizes before unmapping — bare pause is sleep minus the synchronizing half. RL callers pause, run their own weight-sync kernels/NCCL, then sleep; that work races whatever the engine launched last. Reported from production, surviving today only on the incidental ~0.5s between pause and sleep. **2. The pause path launches unwaited GPU work.** `DPEngineCoreProc._pause_complete` kick-starts `engines_running = True` so every rank reaches the consensus all-reduce in `_has_global_unfinished_reqs` — and the fixed every-32-step cadence then forces **32 dummy forwards per rank per pause call** on an idle engine. The final dummy batch is launched in the consensus iteration itself, is not in `batch_queue`, and is invisible to `has_work()`; one iteration later the future resolves while it can still be executing. `wait_for_requests_to_drain()` cannot compensate: the coordinator only tracks request-driven waves, so during the burst it publishes "not running" and drain returns instantly. Measured (DP=2 + EP, PowerMoE-3b, dummy batch inflated to ~110ms to model a large-MoE step): `pause_generation()` on an **idle** engine takes **3.40s** and returns with the device still busy. ## Change A device barrier at pause completion. `WorkerBase.synchronize_device()` synchronizes through the device-generic `torch.accelerator` API whenever an accelerator is registered — the same barrier `sleep()` relies on — so CUDA, XPU and any other `torch.accelerator` backend get it without an override, and it stays a no-op only where there is genuinely no accelerator (CPU); backends outside `torch.accelerator` must override with their own wait. `EngineCore._finish_pause()`: `collective_rpc("synchronize_device")`, *then* cache reset — synchronizing first also stops `clear_cache=True` from resetting state the last launched batch may still be using. Called from all three completion paths (in-proc, fast path, deferred idle callback). `collective_rpc` waits for **all** workers, which also closes `execute_dummy_batch` waiting only for the output rank. The barrier does not shrink the burst itself: an idle-engine DP pause still runs 32 dummy forwards, it just waits for them honestly. #52957 cuts the burst to a single step with a one-condition cadence change; the two PRs compose but neither depends on the other. ## Reproduction (scripts included) Requires 2 GPUs and `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly`. Save the three files below into a directory `$W`, then: ```bash # baseline: the bug docker run --rm --gpus '"device=0,1"' --ipc=host --shm-size=16g \ -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface -v $W:/patch \ --entrypoint bash vllm/vllm-openai:nightly /patch/gpurepro.sh instr # with this PR: check out the branch, then git diff main...HEAD -- vllm/ > $W/fix.patch docker run --rm --gpus '"device=0,1"' --ipc=host --shm-size=16g \ -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface -v $W:/patch \ --entrypoint bash vllm/vllm-openai:nightly /patch/gpurepro.sh fixed ``` (If NCCL fails at init on a CUDA-13.1 driver, add `-e NCCL_NVLS_ENABLE=0`.)
gpupatch.py — instrumentation only: inflates the dummy batch to ~110ms to model a large-MoE step, and adds a device_idle() probe RPC ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Usage: gpupatch.py — instruments a vLLM install.""" import sys site = sys.argv[1] def sub(path, old, new): with open(path) as f: src = f.read() if new in src: return assert old in src and src.count(old) == 1, f"pattern not found/unique in {path}" with open(path, "w") as f: f.write(src.replace(old, new)) OLD = """\ def execute_dummy_batch(self) -> None: num_tokens = getattr(self.model_runner, "uniform_decode_query_len", 1) self.model_runner._dummy_run(num_tokens, uniform_decode=True) """ NEW = """\ def execute_dummy_batch(self) -> None: num_tokens = getattr(self.model_runner, "uniform_decode_query_len", 1) self.model_runner._dummy_run(num_tokens, uniform_decode=True) import os as _os _cycles = int(_os.environ.get("REPRO_SLEEP_CYCLES", "0")) if _cycles: # Simulate a large-MoE forward: keep the stream busy after launch. torch.cuda._sleep(_cycles) def device_idle(self) -> bool: return bool(torch.cuda.current_stream().query()) """ sub(f"{site}/vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py", OLD, NEW) print("instrumented") ```
repro_gpu.py — the scenario: pause / drain / probe ```python import asyncio import time from vllm import SamplingParams from vllm.engine.arg_utils import AsyncEngineArgs from vllm.v1.engine.async_llm import AsyncLLM async def main(): engine = AsyncLLM.from_engine_args( AsyncEngineArgs( model="ibm-research/PowerMoE-3b", data_parallel_size=2, enable_expert_parallel=True, gpu_memory_utilization=0.5, max_model_len=512, enforce_eager=True, ) ) async def gen(rid): async for _ in engine.generate( "The capital of France is", SamplingParams(max_tokens=8), rid ): pass async def probe(tag): idle = await engine.collective_rpc("device_idle") print(f"PROBE {tag}: device_idle={idle}", flush=True) return all(idle) await gen("warmup") await asyncio.sleep(6) await probe("settled") # sanity: True when quiet # scenario 1: pause on a quiet engine t0 = time.perf_counter() await engine.pause_generation(mode="abort") t1 = time.perf_counter() await probe("after_pause1_returned") print(f"S1 pause took {t1 - t0:.2f}s on an idle engine", flush=True) await engine.wait_for_requests_to_drain(60) await probe("after_drain1_returned") # scenario 2: second pause+drain right before sleep (the production recipe) t0 = time.perf_counter() await engine.pause_generation(mode="abort") t1 = time.perf_counter() await probe("after_pause2_returned") await engine.wait_for_requests_to_drain(60) await probe("after_drain2_returned") print(f"S2 second pause took {t1 - t0:.2f}s", flush=True) # scenario 3: drain called while the pause burst is mid-flight await engine.resume_generation() await gen("rearm") await asyncio.sleep(6) task = asyncio.create_task(engine.pause_generation(mode="abort")) await asyncio.sleep(0.8) await engine.wait_for_requests_to_drain(60) idle = await probe("drain_during_pause_burst") print(f"S3 drain returned while pause_done={task.done()}, idle={idle}", flush=True) await task engine.shutdown() asyncio.run(main()) ```
gpurepro.sh — container entrypoint ```bash #!/bin/bash # usage: gpurepro.sh instr|fixed set -x SITE=/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages if [ "$1" = "fixed" ]; then (cd "$SITE" && patch -p1 --forward) < /patch/fix.patch || exit 89 fi python3 /patch/gpupatch.py "$SITE" || exit 90 export REPRO_SLEEP_CYCLES=200000000 # ~110ms on H200 export VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL=WARNING python3 /patch/repro_gpu.py ```
Output on `0.26.1rc1.dev942` (H200): | probe | baseline | this PR | |---|---|---| | device idle when engine settled | True | True | | device idle when `pause_generation()` returns | **False** | **True** | | `pause_generation()` wall time on an *idle* engine | 3.40s | 3.40s (burst kept; #52957 cuts it to 0.17s) | | device idle when drain returns | **False** | **True** | | second pause+drain before sleep | 3.40s, busy | 3.40s, idle | | drain mid-pause | "Engines are idle" while `pause_done=False`, device busy | pause already complete, device idle | ## Test Plan Three unit tests in `tests/v1/engine/test_engine_core.py` (no GPU): the pause-ordering contracts — fast path and deferred path run synchronize → cache reset → future resolution, and overlapping pause calls each complete behind their own barrier. Two adversarial DP tests for edges the pause path crosses that had no coverage: `mode="wait"` draining through the DP consensus path, and pausing a *sleeping* engine — whose ranks skip dummy batches yet must still reach consensus, with the barrier running against unmapped memory. signals.title: [Bugfix] Scan the final window in ASR audio split-point search
signals.text: ## Purpose `find_split_point` (used by `split_audio` for ASR long-audio chunking) scans non-overlapping RMS-energy windows to pick a low-energy split point. The loop bound ```python for i in range(0, len(segment) - min_energy_window, min_energy_window): ``` uses an exclusive stop of `len - min_energy_window`, which drops the final full window `[len - min_energy_window, len)` whenever `len(segment)` is an exact multiple of `min_energy_window`. When the quietest region lies in that final window, it is never scanned, so the search falls back to a louder point and the chunk boundary can cut through speech. Fix: use `len - min_energy_window + 1` as the exclusive stop so the last full window is scanned. ```diff - for i in range(0, len(segment) - min_energy_window, min_energy_window): + for i in range(0, len(segment) - min_energy_window + 1, min_energy_window): ``` ## Not a duplicate Open audio PRs (#48225, #45115, #45063, #35159, #34375, #33564) all address cumulative Whisper **timestamp** drift/offset compensation, and #49414 is docs-only. None modify `find_split_point`'s window-scanning loop / silence detection. ## Test Plan - New regression test `tests/multimodal/test_audio.py::TestAudioChunking::test_find_split_point_scans_final_window`: search region spanning exactly three windows with silence only in the final window; asserts the split lands in that window. - `pytest tests/multimodal/test_audio.py::TestAudioChunking` ## Test Result - Before the fix, the new test **fails** (`assert 0 == 3200` — the silent final window is missed). After the fix it **passes**. - Full `TestAudioChunking` class: **13 passed**. - `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` (v0.14.0) clean on both changed files. ## Model evaluation This change affects only *where* audio is chunked, not model numerics; transcription text may differ only at chunk boundaries. No end-to-end ASR accuracy eval was run (no GPU on hand). Happy to add an ASR eval if maintainers want it. --- AI assistance was used to write this change; a human contributor has reviewed every changed line and run the tests above.

signals.title: [Bugfix][Model][NVIDIA] Fix DeepSeek V4 mHC TileLang warmup for nvidi…
signals.text: [Bugfix][Model][NVIDIA] Fix DeepSeek V4 mHC TileLang warmup for nvidia GPU backend ## Purpose The native `deepseek_v4_mhc_warmup` was a no-op on nvidia GPU (CUDA) models because `_find_first_mhc_layer` required `hc_pre`/`hc_post` CustomOp attributes that the nvidia `DeepseekV4DecoderLayer` does not have — it calls tilelang functions (`mhc_pre_tilelang`, `mhc_pre_broadcast_tilelang`, `mhc_fused_post_pre_tilelang`, `mhc_post_tilelang`, `hc_head_fused_kernel_tilelang`) directly instead of going through CustomOp wrappers. This caused TileLang JIT compilations during inference, creating ~6 second latency spikes on every new token count (up to ~40 minutes of cumulative compilations on a cold start). Fixes #51790. Extends #51802 with full grid coverage. ## Changes 1. **`_find_first_mhc_layer`**: Added dual detection — checks for `hc_pre`/`hc_post` (AMD/XPU CustomOp path) OR `attn_norm`/`ffn_norm` (nvidia tilelang path). Both backends are recognized. 2. **`_warmup_nvidia_layer_mhc`** (new): Warmup path for nvidia models. Calls the same five tilelang functions (`mhc_pre_tilelang`, `mhc_pre_broadcast_tilelang`, `mhc_fused_post_pre_tilelang`, `mhc_post_tilelang`, `hc_head_fused_kernel_tilelang`) that the real `forward()` uses, with actual layer parameters (attention/FFN weights, normalization params, broadcast weights). 3. **`_warmup_hc_head`**: When `hc_head_op` CustomOp is absent (nvidia), falls back to the underlying tilelang function via `_get_tilelang_mhc_ops()`. 4. **Expanded `_DEFAULT_TOKEN_SIZE_CANDIDATES`**: Increased from 15 (powers of 2 only) to 42 values covering all unique grid thresholds for both broadcast (21) and fused (26) n_splits kernels. This ensures every kernel variant is pre-compiled during startup, eliminating runtime TileLang JIT compilations. ## Test Plan ```bash pytest -q tests/model_executor/test_deepseek_v4_mhc_warmup.py ruff check vllm/model_executor/warmup/deepseek_v4_mhc_warmup.py tests/model_executor/test_deepseek_v4_mhc_warmup.py ``` ## Test Result - `pytest` — 6 passed - `ruff check` — passed - **End-to-end validation on NVIDIA GPU:** - Built Docker image with fix, deployed vLLM server (TP=4, EP=4) - Native warmup at startup compiled all 42 token-size variants covering all 21 broadcast + 26 fused n_splits thresholds (previously 0 compilations on nvidia) - After warmup, sent real inference requests (`thinking_token_budget=16000`, `max_tokens=16000`) - **Zero TileLang JIT compilations during inference** — confirmed via `jit_monitor` logs --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [x] The purpose of the PR: fix DeepSeek V4 mHC TileLang warmup being a no-op on nvidia GPU backend, causing ~6s latency spikes during inference - [x] The test plan: pre-commit ruff check, pytest - [x] The test results: ruff passes, all 6 tests pass, all TileLang kernels compile during startup, zero compilations during inference - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update: N/A </details>

signals.title: [Bugfix][Core] Ignore stale KV transfer completions
signals.text: ## Purpose Fix https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/46240 Prevent stale, duplicate, or out-of-order KV transfer completion notifications from crashing the scheduler or freeing blocks owned by a live request. `KVConnectorOutput.finished_recving` and `finished_sending` currently identify a transfer only by request ID. A delayed completion may therefore arrive after the request has been removed, or after the same request has moved into a different lifecycle state. The scheduler currently treats these cases as fatal ownership violations: ```python assert req_id in self.requests assert RequestStatus.is_finished(req.status) ``` This PR makes KV transfer completion handling idempotent and state-aware: - Ignore and log completions for request IDs that no longer exist. - Free blocks when the corresponding request is already finished. - Ignore and log unexpected completions for a live request instead of freeing blocks belonging to its current lifecycle. - Apply the same protection to both receive and send completions. - Add regression tests for unknown request IDs and duplicate/out-of-order completions targeting a running request. ### Duplicate-work check - #46304 overlaps with this PR for completions targeting an already-freed request and the same-step finished_recving/finished_sending case. This PR additionally covers stale or out-of-order completions whose request ID still exists but now belongs to a live lifecycle, such as a request that has already been promoted to RUNNING. In that case, checking only whether the request ID exists is insufficient and may still assert or free live blocks. - #50565 fixes a Mooncake-specific cleanup-only pull after an early abort. It does not cover connector-agnostic delayed or duplicate completion paths ## Test Plan ``` .venv/bin/python -m pytest --noconftest \ tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/test_remote_prefill_lifecycle.py -v ``` ## Test Result --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [ ] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [ ] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [ ] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details>

signals.title: [Core] Sync DP state on the first step of a wave
signals.text: Part of #51476. Independent of #52914 (no shared commits, either can land first): #52914 makes the pause-manufactured GPU work harmless; this PR makes it (nearly) not exist. ## Purpose Pausing an idle MoE DP engine kick-starts every rank into the stepping loop so the ranks can reach the pause-consensus all-reduce — and the fixed every-32-step sync cadence in `_has_global_unfinished_reqs` then forces **32 dummy forwards per rank per pause call** before the pause can complete. For RL post-training, which pauses on every weight sync, that is seconds of latency and pure GPU burn on every training step. Measured with a ~110ms inflated step: `pause_generation()` on an idle DP=2+EP engine takes **3.40s**. The same cost is paid a second time by `sleep()`, which internally re-runs `pause_scheduler` (it must: it is the quiescence consensus for direct-sleep callers and enforces `mode="abort"` semantics on requests kept by a prior `pause(mode="keep")`). This PR caps that redundancy at one dummy step too. The burst cannot simply be skipped per-rank: ranks must enter the blocking gloo all-reduce with equal forward-launch counts, or a peer's in-flight collective waits for a launch that never comes and its host never reaches the all-reduce — distributed deadlock. Any cadence decision must therefore be a pure function of state all ranks observe identically. ## Change One condition: also sync on the **first** step of a wave (`step_counter == 1`), keeping the every-32 cadence afterwards. `step_counter` is already rank-synchronized (reset together at the wave-end consensus, restored by the elastic-EP state sync), so the new cadence remains a pure function of lockstep state — no new state, no protocol change, immune to elastic EP by construction. Effect: an idle-engine pause reaches consensus after **one** dummy forward instead of 32. A mid-wave pause still detects at the next cadence point, but those steps are real serving work. Steady-state serving pays one extra gloo all-reduce per wave, on the step where the wave's first real batch is already running. `step_counter` semantics (+1 per step, reset at wave end) are unchanged; its other consumers (`SchedulerStats.step_counter`, `_should_throttle_prefills`) are unaffected, and `test_dp_prefill_schedule_interval` is included in the runs below. ## Test Plan Two new unit tests (no GPU, scripted `sync_dp_state`): a normal wave syncs at steps {1, 32, 64}; an idle-engine pause (`pending_pause=True`) reaches consensus on step 1 and sets `ignore_start_dp_wave`. Regression: `tests/v1/distributed/test_async_llm_dp.py -k "dp_pause or dp_sleep or prefill_schedule"` — includes the staggered-race and barrier-deadlock guards and the late-request pair from #51481. ```bash python -m pytest tests/v1/engine/test_engine_core.py -k dp_sync -v python -m pytest tests/v1/distributed/test_async_llm_dp.py -k "dp_pause or dp_sleep or prefill_schedule" -v ``` ## Test Result `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly` (`0.26.1rc1.dev942`), A/B in containers on 2×H200 (`patch -p1` of this diff into site-packages; mount the branch's `tests/`). | suite | before (nightly) | after (this PR) | |---|---|---| | `test_engine_core.py -k dp_sync` | **2 failed** | **2 passed** | | `test_async_llm_dp.py` (12 cases) | 12 passed | 12 passed | Pause latency, measured with #52914's barrier applied in both arms (an idle-engine `pause_generation()` on DP=2+EP PowerMoE-3b, dummy step inflated to ~110ms to make the burst visible): | scenario | 32-step cadence | with this PR | |---|---|---| | `pause_generation()` wall time, idle engine | **3.40s** | **0.17s** | | second pause+drain immediately before `sleep()` | 3.40s | **0.20s** | <details> <summary>Reproduction: measure the pause burst (same kit as #52914)</summary> The scripts and container invocation are in the description of #52914 (`gpupatch.py` instruments `execute_dummy_batch` with `torch.cuda._sleep` and a stream-idle probe; `repro_gpu.py` times `pause_generation()` on an idle DP=2 engine and the pause+drain-before-sleep recipe). Run them on bare nightly vs. nightly + this patch to reproduce the 3.40s → 0.17s delta; the per-pause dummy-forward count per rank drops from 32 to 1 in the instrumentation log. </details> ## Essential Elements - Not a duplicate: `gh pr list --search "dp sync cadence"` / `"step_counter pause"` show no open PR touching the DP finish-sync cadence; filed under #51476 as a follow-up alongside #52914. - Control-plane only; no effect on model output, so no eval run is included. - AI assistance was used (Claude; the design was adversarially reviewed with a second model, which surfaced the elastic-EP divergence risk that motivated the stateless form). The submitter has reviewed each changed line and the test runs above.

signals.title: [ROCm][Perf][MiniMax-M3] Optimize sparse GQA prefill attention
signals.text: ## Motivation This kernel spends nearly all its time loading KV blocks, not doing math. On gfx950 a version that only loads the blocks and skips the attention math entirely still takes 103% of the full kernel time. The waste is that neighbouring query tokens pick mostly the same blocks. Four tokens in a row together pick only about 22 distinct blocks, but the kernel loads 64, because it reloads every block once per token. ## Proposed Fix Handle four query tokens per program and load each distinct block once for the whole group. This cuts KV traffic roughly 3x. `topk_idx` is still read per token, so the indexer is untouched. Some layers pick badly enough that the group's block list gets too big to be worth it. Those groups fall back to the original one-token-per-program path. Both kernels launch every time on a fixed grid, and each program compares its own group's list size against 38 to decide whether the group is its own. Nothing is decided on the host, so graph capture still works. The union path is also retuned: `SUB_K` 64 to 32, `num_warps` 4 to 2, and the four-token membership mask now rides in the top bits of the block ID, saving one load per block and one allocation per call. ## Test results Tested on 4 GPUs, gfx950, model -> `amd/MiniMax-M3-MXFP4` Kernel time, median per call across the prefill chunk shapes the server actually produces: | KV cache dtype | Before | After | Speedup | |---|---|---|---| | FP8 | 3.837 ms | 1.849 ms | 2.08x | | BF16 | 3.223 ms | 1.601 ms | 2.01x | Faster in all 16 shape and dtype combinations tested. Output differs from before by at most 4e-3 relative, which is BF16 rounding from reassociating the softmax. End to end, 2 runs per point. Positive throughput and negative latency are better. | KV dtype | Workload | Throughput | TTFT | TPOT | E2EL | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | FP8 | 8k/1k, C8 | +0.34% | -4.78% | +0.09% | -0.34% | | FP8 | 8k/1k, C64 | +2.96% | -5.60% | -2.37% | -2.88% | | FP8 | 60k/600, C16 | +2.44% | -3.98% | -1.45% | -2.38% | | FP8 | 128k/1k, C8 | +1.68% | -2.71% | -0.98% | -1.65% | | BF16 | 8k/1k, C8 | -0.02% | -2.13% | +0.21% | +0.02% | | BF16 | 8k/1k, C64 | +1.25% | -4.41% | -0.68% | -1.24% | | BF16 | 60k/600, C16 | +0.40% | -0.49% | -0.35% | -0.40% | | BF16 | 128k/1k, C8 | +0.08% | -0.35% | +0.10% | -0.07% | ## To-Do Full GSM8K: TODO. <details> <summary>Reproduction command</summary> ```bash export HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3 export VLLM_USE_BREAKABLE_CUDAGRAPH=1 export VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 export VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_MOE=1 export VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTENTION=1 export VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_FUSION_SHARED_EXPERTS=1 export VLLM_ROCM_QUICK_REDUCE_QUANTIZATION=INT4 export VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn export SAFETENSORS_FAST_GPU=1 vllm serve amd/MiniMax-M3-MXFP4 \ --served-model-name minimax-m3 \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --distributed-executor-backend mp \ --trust-remote-code \ --block-size 128 \ --no-enable-prefix-caching \ --language-model-only \ --max-model-len 133120 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 32768 \ --max-num-seqs 128 \ --enable-chunked-prefill \ --async-scheduling \ --attention-backend ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN \ --moe-backend aiter \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --tool-call-parser minimax_m3 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --reasoning-parser minimax_m3 \ --no-enable-log-requests \ --port 8000 ``` ```bash vllm bench serve --backend openai --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \ --endpoint /v1/completions --model amd/MiniMax-M3-MXFP4 \ --served-model-name minimax-m3 --dataset-name random \ --random-input-len 60000 --random-output-len 600 --ignore-eos \ --request-rate inf --max-concurrency 16 --num-prompts 32 --num-warmups 16 --seed 42 ``` </details>

signals.title: [Bugfix][V1] Don't crash the engine on an aborted request
signals.text: ## Purpose I think there is a narrow race condition allowing for an uncaught RuntimeError affecting requests aborted before they've started running. A request can be aborted (e.g. when a client disconnect) via `finish_requests` while still sitting in the scheduler's waiting queue. If it lands between `schedule` popping the request and checking its status, the status is no longer WAITING or PREEMPTED, and `schedule` raises an uncaught RuntimeError. This crashes the entire engine-core process. For vllm-omni the single stage dying dying takes the orchestrator and all other stages down with it (which was how I originally found the issue). I'm not 100% certain this is the correct fix but I tried to split the problem into two pieces * An early check right after `peek_request` drops an already finished request but before any KV cache allocation happens for it. * A second at the original crash site handling the narrower window between the (second) pop_request() and the status check For the second in particular I'm not confident the clean up code is entirely correct and would greatly appreciate some feedback. @njhill ## Test Plan - New regression test, test_schedule_drops_request_aborted_while_waiting in tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.pt that simulating the conditions triggering the trash. - Verified the test fails with the original RuntimeError: Invalid request status: FINISHED_ABORTED traceback against unpatched scheduler.py, and passes with the fix. ## Test Result ================= 131 passed, 16 warnings in 67.08s (0:01:07) ==================

signals.title: [ROCm][aiter] officially supporting aiter Triton kernels+dsv4 on RDNA3
signals.text: ## Purpose Enable the AITER Triton FP8 paths on **RDNA3 / gfx11, bringing it to parity with the gfx12/RDNA4 enablement. This is done by folding gfx11 into the two existing AITER **RDNA** gates rather than sprinkling per-site `gfx11` checks. **Relationship to prior work:** - **Continuation / mirror of #43615**. This PR extends the exact same mechanism to gfx11/RDNA3 — both are RDNA, neither has a CK build, so only aiter's Triton kernels exist on either. Instead of duplicating the gate for a third arch, it switches the two RDNA gates to the canonical `on_rdna()` predicate (`gfx11 + gfx12`, minus CDNA gfx1250), so every downstream site (fp8 MoE oracles, blockscale linear, quant-fusion passes, pass-manager, GDN, sparse-MLA) lights up for gfx11 with no per-site edits. - **Supplement to #47017**. That PR made DSV4 *run* on gfx11 but relied on the op-level **CPU/torch fallback**, without broadly enabling AITER. The usage of "item()" from PyTorch fail cudagraph capture and can only be used with --enforce-eager". This PR removes that torch-fallback dependence for gfx11 by registering **all** aiter ops through the general path and partially reverted the fragile _direct_register_custom_op_(). - **Supersedes #51555** . It adds a *separate* kernel that dequantizes fp8 → bf16 **in-kernel** before `tl.dot`, when the Triton compiler already implicitly does the same work during lowering, after minor fix https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/4764. Simply adapting the Aiter's kernel is cleaner. ## Test Plan Hardware: 8× AMD Radeon Pro W7900 (gfx1100 / RDNA3), TP=8. Model: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731`. `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`. **Online serve + bench** (`vllm serve` + `vllm bench serve`, random dataset), in **both** eager and cudagraph/compiled modes`. Server (cudagraph mode): ```bash VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 --trust-remote-code --max-model-len 2048 \ --max-num-seqs 64 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 --port 8500 ``` Client: ```bash vllm bench serve --backend openai --base-url http://localhost:8500 \ --endpoint /v1/completions --model deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 \ --dataset-name random --random-input-len 128 --random-output-len 256 \ --ignore-eos --request-rate inf --max-concurrency 64 --num-prompts 128 \ --percentile-metrics ttft,tpot,itl,e2el --metric-percentiles 50,90,99 ``` ## Test Result dsv4 runs fine on 8x gfx1100. --- **Not a duplicate:** re-checked against open PRs (`gfx11 aiter`, `rdna3`) on 2026-08-19. No open PR folds gfx11 into the AITER RDNA gates. It mirrors merged #43615, supplements merged #47017, and supersedes open #51555 for the gfx1100 case (see Purpose).

signals.title: [Kimi K3][Pref] Export prefill checkpoints in a single FlashKDA pass
signals.text: ## Purpose This PR adds an optional Kimi-K3 prefill checkpoint mode for fine-grained prefix caching. When enabled, FlashKDA exports an intermediate recurrent-state checkpoint during the prefill. The checkpoint is stored in an internal request-owned Mamba block, allowing prefix cache entries smaller than the Mamba block size to be reused without an additional FlashKDA forward. Main changes: - Export recurrent-state checkpoints from the existing packed FlashKDA prefill. - Export the matching causal-conv state. - Support partial prefix caching. - Add internal checkpoint block allocation, lifecycle management, and scheduler metadata. - Allow the scheduler to skip the additional checkpoint-boundary forward. - Add unit tests for checkpoint metadata, block lifecycle, and prefix caching. [#52789](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52789) introduced the prefill-checkpoint infrastructure. This PR adds efficient support for fine-grained partial prefix caching and exports the checkpoint directly from the existing FlashKDA kernel, avoiding an additional or split FlashKDA forward. ## Usage ```bash VLLM_KIMI_K3_KDA_CHECKPOINT_MODE=1 \ vllm serve <model> \ --kda-prefill-backend flashkda \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --mamba-cache-mode align \ --prefix-match-unit 128 ``` This PR depends on [vllm-project/FlashKDA#7](https://github.com/vllm-project/FlashKDA/pull/7). The FlashKDA commit is temporarily pinned and should be updated after that PR is merged. ## Test Plan Setup: - TP8 on 2 × 4 GB300 - Growing prefix from 120K to 164K tokens - +2K tokens per round - 8 concurrent streams - Three runs per variant ## Test Result | Variant | P50 TTFT | **Improvement** | | --- | ---: | ---: | | #52789, non-partial | 2,151.53 ms | Baseline | | #52789, partial128 | 2,375.23 ms | **-10.40%** | | This PR, non-partial | 2,141.67 ms | Baseline | | **This PR, partial128** | **1,398.49 ms** | **34.70%** | ## Correctness Three consecutive full OCRBench runs with checkpoint mode and partial128 produced: 89.4% 89.6% 89.3% mean: 89.43% --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [ ] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [ ] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [ ] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details>

signals.title: [Bugfix] Prevent stale partial prefix-cache hash resurrection after full-block promotion
signals.text: ## Purpose Fix a bug where `FullAttentionManager._cache_partial_tail_block` re-inserts a superseded partial prefix-cache hash after the owning block has been promoted to a full-block hash. Fixes #49125. ## Root cause `_cache_partial_tail_block` is called on every `cache_blocks()` invocation (i.e. every decode step) with `boundary_tokens` computed from the fixed `request.num_prompt_tokens`. After `super().cache_blocks()` promotes the block to a full-block hash, the `already_cached` guard in `cache_partial_block` evaluates to `False` because the partial hash was removed from the map during promotion — so the stale partial hash gets re-inserted, creating a zombie entry in `cached_block_hash_to_block` and `cached_block_hashes_by_block`. ## Fix Add an early return in `_cache_partial_tail_block` when the target block's `block_hash_num_tokens` already covers at least as many tokens as `boundary_tokens`, indicating the block has been promoted. ## Why not a duplicate of #49145 PR #49145 attempted the same fix but was closed on 2026-08-18 due to unresolved merge conflicts without any maintainer review. This PR is opened against current main (`583a00257d`). ## Tests Added `test_cache_blocks_does_not_resurrect_stale_partial_hash_after_promotion` to `tests/v1/core/prefix_cache/test_partial_prefix_cache_primitives.py`, parametrized over `dcp_world_size` ∈ {1, 2, 4}. ``` PYTHONPATH=tests:. python -m pytest tests/v1/core/prefix_cache/ tests/v1/core/test_single_type_kv_cache_manager.py -x -q 61 passed in 12.54s ``` ## AI assistance This PR was developed with AI assistance (Claude). All code has been reviewed and is understood and owned by the human submitter end-to-end. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signals.title: [K3] Optimize K3 recover ssm kernel times
signals.text: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Purpose PR #51855 added an option to use the ReplaySSM-like recover method. But the new approach, although improving memory footprint and so occupancy, actually hurt run time. The approach should be faster, but it is simple triton vs highly optimized non-triton. Here we make some small tweaks to improve the new output-only verify kernel and the kda and convolution end-of-step commit kernels. ## Test Plan No new tests. This just changes kernel internals and reorders two kernels so are covered by existing tests. We also wrote some one-off checkers that, on fake input, found the output within expected numerical differences (due to changes in associativity) from the old kernels. @benchislett has offered to run e2e tests. ## Test Result TBD --- We make a few simple changes that result in a substantial speedup. ### For commit: The biggest is that we change the KDA recover from a backward recurrence to a forward recurrence, which is the bulk of the speedup. This also lets us save register state when operating in ALIGN_MODE (for prefix caching). We reorder the computation to go plan -> kda commit -> conv commit, vs the more natural plan -> conv commit -> kda commit, and then add PDL between kda and conv. This lets us overlap kda with conv, especially as while they both depend on plan, neither depends on the other for inputs and they have separate outputs. And as kda blocks are longer-tailed the re-reordering is beneficial. Lastly, for both kernels we retune num-warps and the number of output elements each handles. ALIGNED_MODE on and off want slightly different values. To guide optimization we wrote a microbenchmark (not submitted) and optimized for B300, matching the original PRs experiment. We can only match the original PR numbers if we assume that the original PR was actually run with the kernels in unaligned mode. Our microbenchmark assumes TP=8, times the span from plan start to end of the second of conv or kda commit, simulates cold and hot cache inputs, and runs with a cuda graph and CUPTI timing. For ease of experimentation we had all requests uniform in terms of # accepted (using 5 below, slightly higher than the 4.2 average in the e2e nsys measurements in the original PR), and also uniform in bondary behavior. We observed runtime affine in # accepted, as expected (not shown). We ran in either unaligned, aligned with no boundary crossed, or aligned with boundary crossed at the second token. The latter case would never happen at larger batches, we would expect a mix of aligned and unaligned, but it shows the costs. We get a > 2x speedup across all measured batch sizes and boundary conditions. Our PR: | Mode | B1 | B32 | B256 | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Unaligned | 31.72 | 755.81 | 6128.89 | | Aligned, no boundary | 40.01 | 971.00 | 7921.03 | | Aligned, boundary at accepted token 2 | 44.79 | 1157.97 | 9392.93 | Original: | Mode | B1 | B32 | B256 | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Unaligned | 64.67 | 1615.72 | 13092.84 | | Aligned, no boundary | 84.67 | 2281.48 | 18976.55 | | Aligned, boundary at accepted token 2 | 88.53 | 2393.79 | 20051.55 | ### For verify: Small changes here but surprisingly worth a lot. We had a similar microbenchmark as above but for verify. PDL surprisingly hurts us, so we report only the kernel time, not the span, although we ran and timed the conv1d -> verify span. We hoisted dt_bias out of the loop, which resulted in enough code gen change to be worth a win. Then we retuned the value-slice and num_warp params. We found value-slice should vary with batch size, which is typical as smaller value slices are less efficient but better saturate the machine if there isn't enough work. And that num-warps should be 1 everywhere. Also added some cache hints as state and V are not shared across blocks (value slicing) but everything else is. Here are timings, again B300, TP=8, with T=8 and gate_lower_bound=5.0: | Batch | Old | New | Speedup | |---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 13.79 µs | 8.98 µs | 1.54× | | 2 | 13.95 µs | 9.38 µs | 1.49× | | 4 | 14.24 µs | 10.08 µs | 1.41× | | 8 | 15.46 µs | 13.22 µs | 1.17× | | 16 | 27.46 µs | 18.98 µs | 1.45× | | 32 | 41.55 µs | 34.40 µs | 1.21× | | 64 | 79.49 µs | 63.49 µs | 1.25× | | 128 | 147.89 µs | 111.50 µs | 1.33× | | 256 | 306.19 µs | 233.17 µs | 1.31× | | 512 | 632.17 µs | 494.05 µs | 1.28× | Surprises: Passing gate lower bound does change the results a little. As noted above, PDL does not help. A tiny bit in some places but regresses enough others that I left it off, vs making it a heuristic. I also spent a while trying to get a good result with a full chunk/prefill-style UT transform, in Triton, having had good results with that for Mamba-2 layers. Whether due to the per-channel decay (unlikely) or the triangular inverse (likely), I found many bad ways to write it, and with a lot of work I got a version that (for T=8) only tied the recurrence above. I expected big wins, but Triton limitations make it quite challenging. I'm sure in CuTe it'd be very fast. As is, it would have the cost and benefit that the runtime would be independent of T. But as it is much more complicated, and as T=8 is probably more of an upper than lower bound for draft_length + 1, better to stick with the recurrence. AI Declaration: AI assisted in the writing of this code, but I have reviewed every line. Full disclosure, I reviewed all the code in the PR, but the one-off microbenchmarks and such I did not look at too carefully. <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [x] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [x] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [x] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [x] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details> **BEFORE SUBMITTING, PLEASE READ <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/contributing>** (anything written below this line will be removed by GitHub Actions)

signals.title: [CI][Docker] Pin manylinux2_28-builder:cuda13.0 to the release/2.13 image
signals.text: ## Purpose `BUILD_BASE_IMAGE` currently tracks the floating tag `pytorch/manylinux2_28-builder:cuda13.0`. That tag is rebuilt upstream, so the compiler, glibc and CUDA toolchain underneath every CUDA 13.0 wheel build can change without a single vLLM commit. The practical cost is attribution: the same vLLM SHA can build one day and fail the next, and bisecting vLLM will never find the cause because nothing in vLLM changed. This pins it to `cuda13.0-78e737ad29420ffc4800e677c51e2a852caf8359` — the exact image PyTorch's own `release/2.13` branch uses in `.github/workflows/generated-linux-binary-manywheel-nightly.yml` (commit `78e737ad`, 2026-06-26). So vLLM builds against an immutable toolchain that is known-good because it is the one a shipped PyTorch release was built with. ## Changes Five references to the bare x86 CUDA 13.0 tag: | File | What | |---|---| | `docker/Dockerfile` | `ARG BUILD_BASE_IMAGE` default | | `docker/versions.json` | regenerated with `tools/generate_versions_json.py` (not hand-edited) | | `.buildkite/image_build/image_build_torch_nightly.sh` | `NIGHTLY_BUILD_BASE_IMAGE` | | `.buildkite/release-pipeline.yaml` | x86 nightly wheel build + two `vllm-openai` image builds | ## Deliberately not changed - **`manylinuxaarch64-builder:cuda13.0`** (arm64 build, GH200 test script, docs) and **`manylinux2_28-builder:cuda12.9`** — different images. Pinning them is worth doing, but each needs its own known-good tag chosen the same way; I did not want to guess at those in this PR. - The `registry.acme.org/mirror/...` example comment in `docker/Dockerfile`, which documents repository renaming for private mirrors. Pinning it there would make the example about something else. ## Test Plan - `docker/versions.json` was regenerated by the repo's own generator rather than edited by hand; the one-line diff confirms no other drift. - CI on this PR exercises the pinned image directly: any CUDA 13.0 x86 build step that succeeds is evidence the tag resolves and builds. ## Test Result Pending CI. ## Note Worth deciding as a policy question, not just for this PR: whether vLLM wants to track the floating tag deliberately (early warning of upstream toolchain changes, at the cost of unattributable breakage) or pin and bump on purpose. This PR takes the second position for the x86 CUDA 13.0 path only. If maintainers prefer the first, the same argument says the pin should at least be applied on release branches.

Track a separate DSpark draft-input budget so each stage can use the configured batch capacity without exceeding it. This does not duplicate an open PR. Searches for #52922 and for DSpark scheduling found no open PR addressing this accounting bug. Credit to @slippersss for reporting the bug and providing the minimal scheduling example. AI assistance was used to investigate, implement, test, and write this change. The human submitter must review every changed line and reproduce the tests before submission. ## Test Plan - Add a scheduler regression test for two 8-token prefills with a 16-token target budget and four DSpark query tokens per request. - Check that the independent draft budget still limits five one-token requests to four admitted requests. - Run the full core scheduler test file. - Run pre-commit on both changed files. ## Test Result Tested on Linux with Python 3.12.13. The node has eight NVIDIA A40 GPUs, but the scheduler tests used the CPU backend. - Regression test without the fix: 1 failed, 1 passed. The second prefill received 2 tokens instead of 8. - Focused tests with the fix: 3 passed. - `tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py`: 149 passed. - Pre-commit on both changed files: passed. No DSpark model was loaded, and no GPU end-to-end generation was run. signals.title: [Distributed] Enable FlashInfer all-reduce by default
signals.text: ## Purpose Enable the existing FlashInfer all-reduce backend by default for tensor-parallel CUDA groups. The existing platform, world-size, tensor-shape, and workspace guards remain in place, so unsupported calls continue through the normal all-reduce fallback chain. `VLLM_ALLREDUCE_USE_FLASHINFER=0` remains available as an explicit opt-out. FlashInfer all-reduce is always excluded when `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` because it does not provide the fixed reduction order that batch invariance requires. ## Duplicate-work check No issue number was provided, so the issue-number lookup was not applicable. I searched open PRs for `FlashInfer All Reduce`, `FlashInfer allreduce`, `VLLM_ALLREDUCE_USE_FLASHINFER`, and `FlashInfer default allreduce`. The related open PRs cover benchmark initialization (#40970), MNNVL workspace capacity (#50932), topology fallback (#48075), and batch-invariant fused all-reduce behavior (#51292). #50505 includes the same communicator exclusion as part of a broader redesign of batch-invariant custom all-reduce; this PR only carries the guard required to make the default flip safe. None of these PRs changes this environment variable's default. ## Tests ```bash .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_envs.py -q # 56 passed .venv/bin/python -m pytest \ 'tests/distributed/test_comm_ops.py::test_multi_process_tensor_parallel[test_target0-2]' -v # 1 passed on 2x NVIDIA GB200 VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 .venv/bin/python -m pytest \ 'tests/distributed/test_comm_ops.py::test_multi_process_tensor_parallel[test_target0-2]' -v -s # 1 passed on 2x NVIDIA GB200 .venv/bin/pre-commit run --files \ vllm/envs.py \ vllm/distributed/device_communicators/cuda_communicator.py # all applicable hooks passed ``` ## Model evaluation Ran `facebook/opt-125m` with TP=2, FP16, eager mode, greedy decoding, and the prompt `The capital of France is` on 2x NVIDIA GB200: - Unset/default: logs selected `FLASHINFER` and initialized the `mnnvl` workspace; token IDs were `[5, 812, 9, 5, 1515, 3497, 4, 50118]`. - `VLLM_ALLREDUCE_USE_FLASHINFER=0`: logs excluded `FLASHINFER`; token IDs were identical. - `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 VLLM_ALLREDUCE_USE_FLASHINFER=1`: logs selected only `PYNCCL`; token IDs were identical. No performance benchmark was run. ## AI assistance OpenAI Codex assisted with implementation, tests, validation, and drafting this description. This is a draft PR; the human submitter must review every changed line and confirm they understand and can defend the change before marking it ready for review.

signals.title: Fix multicast mailbox publication
signals.text: <!-- markdownlint-disable --> ## Purpose Fix silent output corruption in vLLM's MNNVL Lamport all-gather. CUDA multicast addresses refer to one symmetric buffer replicated across GPUs, and CUDA requires `multimem.*` to write them. The existing ordinary store has undefined behavior and can become visible late or partially, leaving peers to assemble incorrect hidden-state chunks that attention turns into fluent but unrelated text ([PTX ISA](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/#data-movement-and-conversion-instructions-multimem-ld-reduce-multimem-st-multimem-red)). DeepSeek-V4 with MegaMoE, expert parallelism, and TP8 reaches this kernel through sequence-parallel all-gather and reduce-scatter. Publish each mailbox entry with a system-scope release multicast store, order the multicast and local virtual-address aliases with `fence.proxy.alias`, and poll the local copy with acquire loads ([CUDA virtual aliasing](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/04-special-topics/virtual-memory-management.html#virtual-aliasing-support)). Clean the previously used mailbox stage rather than the stage used by the next epoch, so a slow rank cannot erase data that a faster peer has already published. The architecture guard limits multicast dispatch to CUDA 12.1+ SM90 targets and traps outside that contract. This also adds a real-GPU regression test to the existing 2×B200 distributed CI job. A passing B200 run on the old code is plausible because the observed symptom is topology- and timing-sensitive and has manifested on multi-node GB300; B200 still provides path coverage and an exact correctness oracle, while a multi-node MNNVL pool provides the stronger red-before/green-after test. Open-PR searches for MNNVL Lamport, CUDA multicast, and multimem publication found this fix to be unique. ## Test Plan Run kernel-level validation on GB300 and H100, assert a nonzero CUDA multicast pointer and positive MNNVL Lamport selection, and check exact all-gather and reduce-scatter results for FP32, FP16, and BF16 across multiple shapes, repeated mailbox-stage reuse, and CUDA-graph replay with changing inputs. Inject rank skew after publication to verify that next-stage cleanup fails and previous-stage cleanup remains correct. End-to-end validation used two simple semantic probes whose expected answers are unambiguous: - “What color is the sky on a clear day? One word.” Expected: `Blue` or `Azure`. - “A bat and a ball cost $1.10 total; the bat costs $1 more. How much is the ball?” Expected: `$0.05` or `5 cents`. ## Test Result - Two-GPU GB300 kernel validation selected both MNNVL Lamport kernels and passed exact eager and CUDA-graph comparisons. - Two-node GB300 TP8 rank-skew validation reproduced sentinel/stale-generation corruption with next-stage cleanup and passed with previous-stage cleanup. - Two-node GB300 TP8 DeepSeek-V4 validation: sky-color 10/10 and bat-and-ball 10/10 before and after load; every response matched the expected answer. - GB300 TP4 one-node and two-node controls: both probes 10/10. - H100 SM90 validation: four shapes, each with 100 eager and 100 CUDA-graph iterations, exactly matching NCCL. - The final warmed TP8 run completed 128/128 requests with zero errors at 941.19 output tok/s, showing no performance regression. AI assistance was used during investigation and implementation; the human submitter reviewed the change and owns the design and validation. --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [x] The purpose and root cause are described. - [x] The test plan describes real-GPU coverage. - [x] The test results include kernel and end-to-end validation. - [x] Documentation impact was considered; the code and test fully describe this kernel-only change. </details> **BEFORE SUBMITTING, PLEASE READ <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/contributing>** (anything written below this line will be removed by GitHub Actions)

signals.title: [ROCm][Spec Decode] Add Aiter MLA decode support non-causal draft block
signals.text: ## Purpose On ROCm a Kimi-K3 DSpark draft has to be pinned to TritonMLA: ``` --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","model":"/draft", "num_speculative_tokens":7, "attention_backend":"TRITON_MLA"}' ``` The draft's query block is non-causal. On ROCm only TritonMLA sets `supports_non_causal_multi_token_decode`, so the pin. TritonMLA and FlashInferMLA serve such a block by flattening it: one decode row per query token, every row reading the same committed KV. That is cheap for them because their kernels take a block table, so flattening is a `repeat_interleave`. AiterMLA's kernel takes a flat page-size-1 index list instead. Flattening there means rebuilding that list every forward -- roughly half a million entries at batch 8, block 8 and an 8k context. **Fix: don't flatten. Pass the mask, which the kernel already accepts.** `get_mla_metadata_v1` has always taken `is_causal`. aiter's `mla_decode_fwd` takes `causal` as of v0.1.20. vLLM hardcoded the first and never passed the second: ```python get_mla_metadata_v1(..., self._num_attention_heads, 1, True, ...) # <- the mask ``` Both now get the real value. Same one row per request, same index list. Three pieces make that safe. **Selection.** AiterMLA offers a non-causal block only if the installed `mla_decode_fwd` takes `causal`. Probed by signature, the same way this file already probes for fp8 scale support. **Routing.** Gluon's mask is causal and cannot be turned off, so `use_gluon_verify` now returns False for any non-causal block. Such a block takes the padded asm decode instead. Padding the head count up is what gives it a kernel there -- the fp8 path already relies on that. This is also what lets a bf16 cache serve a non-causal block at all. Builder and impl call the same predicate, so they cannot disagree. **Build.** Two shapes still reach `_build_decode` and it raises for both. One is a block that missed the persistent schedule. The other is an fp8 2-token block: aiter's dispatch has no fold for that length, so the lookup lands on a causal-only kernel. The bf16 fold has no such hole. Outside ROCm, `_build_decode` gains a `causal` kwarg in `MLACommonMetadataBuilder`. The FlashAttn, FlashInfer, FlashMLA and Dots3Note overrides are signature-only updates. DCP is untouched; `supports_non_causal_multi_token_dcp` stays False. vLLM pins aiter **v0.1.19** (`docker/Dockerfile.rocm_base`). That build has no `causal` argument, so **on the default image this PR is a no-op**: `supports_non_causal()` returns False, selection keeps handing the draft group to TritonMLA, and the recipe keeps its pin. It starts working once the pin moves. ## Test Plan ```bash pytest tests/v1/attention/test_rocm_aiter_mla_non_causal.py # 15, CPU only ``` They stub `aiter.mla`, so both aiter generations can be exercised on one machine. The two `_build_decode` guards are covered in `test_rocm_aiter_mla_mtp_split.py`. That file already drives the method directly. End to end on 8x MI355X, `/model` = Kimi-K3 and `/draft` its DSpark draft. Same server twice; the only difference is whether the draft is pinned: ```bash vllm serve /model --served-model-name k3 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 --trust-remote-code \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --max-model-len 16384 --max-num-seqs 128 --max-num-batched-tokens 16384 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.93 --block-size 128 --no-enable-prefix-caching \ --load-format auto --mm-encoder-tp-mode data \ --safetensors-load-strategy prefetch \ --compilation-config '{"custom_ops":["+fused_rms_norm_gated"]}' \ --speculative-config "$SPEC" --port 8000 # A -- what the recipe does today SPEC='{"method":"dspark","model":"/draft","num_speculative_tokens":7,"attention_backend":"TRITON_MLA"}' # B -- this PR: no pin, the draft picks AiterMLA SPEC='{"method":"dspark","model":"/draft","num_speculative_tokens":7}' ``` Drop `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` and run again for the bf16 numbers. That run also needs #50619, for an unrelated main-branch cudagraph defect in the target's causal verify. Both were served against a v0.1.19 install with v0.1.20's MLA files copied in. That install reproduces a full v0.1.20 tree's kernel numbers bit for bit. ```bash for C in 1 8; do vllm bench serve --backend openai-chat --endpoint /v1/chat/completions \ --model k3 --tokenizer /model --trust-remote-code --port 8000 \ --dataset-name random --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 128 \ --ignore-eos --max-concurrency $C --num-prompts $((C == 1 ? 16 : 48)) done lm_eval --model local-chat-completions \ --model_args model=k3,base_url=http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions,num_concurrent=32,tokenized_requests=False \ --tasks gsm8k --num_fewshot 5 --batch_size 32 \ --apply_chat_template --gen_kwargs temperature=0 ``` ## Test Result Unit tests: **15 + 46 passed**. Both runs land on `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` with no cudagraph downgrade. Unpinning drops the second attention backend. So the gap below is the draft's backend and nothing else. | draft backend | conc. | output throughput | mean TPOT | |---|---|---|---| | TritonMLA (pinned) | 1 | 68.44 tok/s | 13.23 ms | | AiterMLA (this PR) | 1 | **76.32 tok/s** | **11.67 ms** | | TritonMLA (pinned) | 8 | 294.57 tok/s | 23.32 ms | | AiterMLA (this PR) | 8 | **324.44 tok/s** | **21.26 ms** | That is 11.5% at concurrency 1 and 10.1% at 8. A bf16 cache reaches 84.16 tok/s at concurrency 1 and 331.66 at 8, TPOT 10.45 ms and 20.76 ms. Accuracy, full GSM8K test set (1319 questions), 5-shot, greedy, fp8 KV: | | flexible-extract | strict-match | |---|---|---| | TritonMLA (pinned), fp8 | 0.9644 ± 0.0051 | 0.9636 ± 0.0052 | | AiterMLA (this PR), fp8 | 0.9613 ± 0.0053 | 0.9606 ± 0.0054 | | AiterMLA (this PR), bf16 | 0.9644 ± 0.0051 | 0.9636 ± 0.0052 | At the kernel, checked with ad-hoc scripts rather than in-tree tests: With an fp8 cache and 16 heads, `causal=False` lands 7.1e-03 from a non-causal reference. Against a causal one it sits 6.3e-02 away at block 4 and 9.1e-02 at block 8. So it runs the mask that was asked for. Four identical query rows come back identical, spread 0.0. With a bf16 cache the padded asm decode holds 3.5e-04 to 5.6e-04. That is across 8, 12, 16, 24 and 32 heads, and block lengths 1 through 16. fp8 covers 1 and 3 through 16. --- Written with AI assistance (Claude Code); the commit carries `Co-authored-by: Claude`. signals.title: [Bugfix][Spec Decode] Use group geometry for FlashAttention metadata
signals.text: ## Summary Use each FlashAttention metadata builder's own attention group as the source of truth for attention geometry: - query heads come from the registered attention layers - KV heads and head size come from the group's `AttentionSpec` - DFlash shallow-copies `VllmConfig` only to override causality, avoiding validator re-entry This prevents FA3 AOT scheduler metadata from being planned with target-model shapes when a draft model has a different GQA ratio. It also handles models with non-uniform per-layer query-head counts without adding `num_q_heads` across the KV-cache specification hierarchy. ## Root cause Draft and target attention groups have separate builders, but the FlashAttention builder read Q/KV/head geometry from the model-wide target `ModelConfig`. FA3 uses those values to construct scheduler metadata while the kernel sees the draft Q/K/V tensor shapes, so different draft/target geometry can produce incompatible scheduler metadata. Current main already splits groups by the registered layers' query-head count and exposes KV geometry through each group's `AttentionSpec`, so the builder can consume those existing local sources directly. This is the current-main replacement for the shape/config concerns in #39775 and #50694. The authors were contacted privately; the older drafts also contain routing and schema changes that current main no longer needs. Addresses #50851. ## Validation - `.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_autoregressive_speculator.py tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash_causality.py tests/v1/attention/test_group_head_counts.py -q` - 29 passed, 4 platform-skipped - `uvx ruff check` on all changed files - `uvx ruff format --check` on all changed files - `git diff --check` The regression test uses conflicting target and draft/group geometry (48/8/128 versus 16/2/64) and verifies FA3 plans with 16/2/64. Model evaluation was not run in the local environment. H200 FA3 serving/evaluation with a mismatched draft/target pair should be completed before marking this PR ready. ## AI assistance AI assistance was used to investigate and implement this change. The submitter will review every changed line and remains responsible for the contribution before marking it ready.

In this PR, I have trimmed the number of parameterizations down to 480, and I've also removed the per-test global cleanup in favor of a single cleanup at the end of the module. Now, the runtime for this test is about 6 minutes locally. I have completely removed the `use_shuffle_kv_layout` parameter since all nonzero cases were being skipped, so we only test with `use_shuffle_kv_layout=0`. I've also reduced `rms_norm_eps` to only one case, `1e-6`, as testing `1e-5` as well provides no practical benefit. Finally, I've chosen to reduce the set of parameters for `num_tokens` from `[5, 16, 2048]` to just `[5, 2048]`. signals.title: [Bugfix] Fix int4 MoE tuner crash on the CUDA wna16 path
signals.text: Fixes #52845. `benchmark_moe.py --tune --dtype int4_w4a16` aborts on the first config on NVIDIA. The tuner skips block-shape filtering for int4 because the Triton `gptq_awq` kernel accepts any `BLOCK_SIZE_K`. But dispatch also selects the CUDA `moe_wna16_gemm` kernel for small batches, and that one asserts `BLOCK_SIZE_K % group_size == 0`, `BLOCK_SIZE_M <= 64`, and `BLOCK_SIZE_K / group_size ∈ {1,2,4,8}`. This restricts the search space to configs that kernel accepts, and only for the batch sizes where `should_moe_wna16_use_cuda()` is true — the Triton path keeps the full space. ## Test ```bash python benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_moe.py \ --model Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-GPTQ-Int4 --tp-size 1 \ --dtype int4_w4a16 --tune --batch-size 1 8 32 ``` Before: `RuntimeError: moe_wna16_gemm ... BLOCK_SIZE_K must divisible by group_size` on config 1/1920. After: completes and writes `E=128,N=768,device_name=NVIDIA_GeForce_RTX_5080,dtype=int4_w4a16.json`. Verified on an RTX 5080 (sm_120), vLLM 0.27.1, torch 2.13.0+cu130.

signals.title: Fix response_format strict=false for Chat Completions and Responses API
signals.text: ## Summary `response_format` affects two independent stages of a request: 1. **Prompt rendering** — the renderer embeds the schema as an instruction in the prompt (input side), so the model knows what format is expected. 2. **Constrained generation** — a grammar engine restricts which tokens can be produced so the output is guaranteed to match the schema (output side). `json_schema.strict=false` means "prompt instruction only": the schema should still be rendered into the prompt, but no grammar constraint should be applied to generation, and the output is not guaranteed to match the schema. **Chat Completions** - Bug: `structured_outputs_from_response_format()` always applied a grammar constraint for `json_schema`, even when `strict=false`. - Fix: return early when `json_schema.strict` is `False`, so no grammar override is applied and any existing `structured_outputs` on the request is preserved. Prompt rendering was already correct (`response_format` reaches renderers via `build_chat_params()`). **Responses API** - Bug: `build_chat_params()` never forwarded `text.format` into `ChatParams.response_format`, so renderers (e.g. Kimi K3) never saw the schema in the prompt at all, regardless of `strict`. - Fix: add `text_config_to_response_format()` to convert the flat Responses `text.format` into the nested `ResponseFormat` shape that renderers expect (the same internal type Chat Completions already populates), and pass it through `build_chat_params()`. - Bug: `extract_structured_outputs()` ignored `strict=false` and always applied a grammar constraint when a schema was present. - Fix: skip the grammar constraint when `text.format.strict` is `False`. ## Test plan - [x] `pytest tests/entrypoints/openai/test_response_format.py -q` (14 passed) - [x] pre-commit: ruff-check, ruff-format, typos, check-spdx-header on changed files

signals.title: [Bugfix] Fix ncclCommQueryProperties heap overflow with NCCL >= 2.31
signals.text: This PR is for fixing host heap corruption (flaky SIGSEGV) when running vLLM with NCCL >= 2.31, seen in multi-node expert-parallel serving (vLLM + DeepEP). `ncclCommQueryProperties` fills the `ncclCommProperties` struct based on the version the caller declares in `props.version`. It never reads `props.size`. C callers get this right through `NCCL_COMM_PROPERTIES_INITIALIZER`, which declares the `NCCL_VERSION_CODE` of the headers the application was compiled against, i.e. the layout its buffer actually has. vLLM instead declared the runtime library version (`ncclGetRawVersion()`) while its ctypes struct only mirrored the NCCL 2.30 layout (56 bytes). NCCL 2.31 grew the struct to 144 bytes (`commHash`, `ginMinStride`, `ginConnectionType`, `ginSupport[64]`, `devCommRuntimeVersionSize`) behind a `props->version >= NCCL_VERSION(2, 31, 0)` gate, so with a 2.31 library vLLM passes the gate and NCCL writes 88 bytes past the end of the buffer. The corruption surfaces later as flaky SIGSEGV or glibc heap errors in unrelated code, once per worker process. This PR extends the ctypes struct to the NCCL 2.31 layout as shipped in v2.31.2-1 (144 bytes, offsets verified against its `nccl_device/core.h`) and clamps the declared `props.version` to the version of the headers the layout was taken from (`NCCL_COMM_PROPERTIES_LAYOUT_VERSION = 23102`), matching the C initializer semantics. The clamp is what prevents this bug class from recurring: when a future NCCL adds fields behind a newer gate, the declared version will not pass that gate, so NCCL will not write fields the buffer does not have. Older NCCL libraries are unaffected because the declared version never exceeds the runtime version.

signals.title: [Bugfix] Avoid eager torch.compile in Kimi K2.5 vision helper
signals.text: ## Problem `get_rope_shape` in the Kimi K2.5 vision encoder is decorated with bare `torch.compile`, and an eager wrapper invokes it on the first input key. signals.title: [Feature][Model Runner V2] Support extract_hidden_states with pipeline parallelism
signals.text: > Superseded by [zupengwang/vllm#1](https://github.com/zupengwang/vllm/pull/1), > which targets the head branch of #49811 directly and therefore shows only > the PP extension. This upstream draft can be recreated after #49811 merges. ## Purpose Depends on #49811. #49811 adds `extract_hidden_states` support to Model Runner V2, but keeps the existing pipeline-parallel restriction for auxiliary hidden-state outputs. This PR extends that implementation to pipeline parallelism. The generic PP path: - initializes the extraction speculator on every PP rank; - maps configured global capture IDs to the PP rank that owns each boundary; - lets non-final stages return their local auxiliary states alongside `IntermediateTensors`; - writes each rank's local states into the corresponding global cache slots; - preserves the PP restriction for EAGLE3, DFlash, and DSpark. Auxiliary tensors are not forwarded through the PP communication path. Each stage caches the boundaries it owns. This also fixes hidden-state cache block sizing for hybrid models. The cache block must divide the existing scheduler block size, which is the LCM of the hybrid groups' block sizes. Using their GCD can collapse the hidden-state block size and substantially over-allocate memory for long contexts. ### Kimi-K3 special case Kimi-K3's AttnRes capture at a PP boundary is defined by the next decoder layer's normalization and projection weights. Those weights normally live on the next PP stage. The preceding stage therefore keeps local copies of the two unsharded vectors when its `end_layer` is selected for capture. There is one additional handoff detail: when a stage starts in the middle of an AttnRes block, the incoming hidden state already includes the pending delta. The receiving stage supplies a zero delta so it follows the normal AttnRes path without applying that contribution twice. Both behaviors are contained in the Kimi-K3 model implementation; the generic MRV2 PP code has no Kimi-specific branching. This provides the MRV2 PP extraction path needed to continue investigating #52909. It does not claim to fix the underlying chunked-prefill issue. AI assistance was used to help implement and validate this change. The submitter reviewed the changed code and understands the implementation. ## Test Plan ```bash git diff --check python -m pytest -q \ tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_extract_hidden_states_speculator.py \ tests/models/kimi_k3/test_pp_handoff.py python -m pytest -q \ tests/v1/core/test_kv_cache_utils.py \ -k hidden_state_group ``` ## Test Results - MRV2 extraction and Kimi-K3 PP boundary tests: `8 passed`. - Hybrid hidden-state cache tests: `2 passed, 80 deselected`. - `git diff --check`: passed. - A derived ARM64 CUDA 13 image was built with an embedded source manifest and verified runtime-file hashes. The final 16-GPU qualification (one 32K request, both one-shot and forced 4x8K chunked prefill, including PP-boundary and final-layer captures) is still pending. This PR is intentionally a draft until that result is available. --- <details> <summary>Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist</summary> - [x] The purpose and dependency are included. - [x] Generic PP behavior and the model-specific Kimi-K3 behavior are separated. - [x] The test plan and current test results are included. - [x] Remaining qualification work is stated explicitly. </details>

signals.title: Add NIXL side channel advertize address for NAT'd deployments
signals.text: ## Purpose VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_HOST is currently used both to bind a NIXL connector instance's local ZMQ metadata handshake listener and as the address advertized to remote peers. There are not always the same address. A producer may need to bind to a local or internal address while being reached by remote peers at a different address. This causes disaggregated P/D serving across two independently administered sites with at least one site using NAT'd OpenStack cloud to fail. Adding a VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_ADVERTIZE_HOST can separate these two needs. ## Test Plan Testing this with prefill server at ACCESS JetStream2 (Indiana University data center) and decode server at CloudLab University of Utah). ## Test Result **Before this fix**, decode's ZMQ metadata handshake against prefill consistently failed with "zmq.error.Again", with "remote_host": "localhost" visible in the failure context. Error message: [distributed/.../nixl/base_worker.py:933] NIXL transfer failure: handshake_failed | Context: {'failure_type': 'handshake_failed', 'request_id': 'cmpl-23c48056-34fc-43fe-aaa7-426c9f953482-0-b5301f64', 'engine_id': 'a56e21d3-56dd-42f5-9398-8ba696988a85', 'remote_engine_id': '47c9c929-8e63-460d-a89c-d1b0010ea088', 'remote_request_id': 'cmpl-23c48056-34fc-43fe-aaa7-426c9f953482-0-9d20b39c', **'remote_host': 'localhost',** 'remote_port': 5559, 'num_local_blocks': 4, 'num_remote_blocks': 4, 'local_block_ids_sample': [1, 2]} **After this fix**, setting VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_HOST=0.0.0.0 (bind) and VLLM_NIXL_SIDE_CHANNEL_ADVERTIZE_HOST=<public_IP> , the error is fixed: the metadata handshake roundtrip dropped from a 5s timeout failure to ~0.16s success, with the public IP now showing up correctly in the handshake payload ("remote_host": <public IP>) ....., 'e5c907ed-a5a7-4b05-85e2-fcd507bbac7f', 'remote_request_id': 'cmpl-93c8ca93-183d-431f-bd12-546c50a83532-0-b4a296ad', **'remote_host': '149.165.172.72',** 'remote_port': 5559, 'num_local_blocks': 4, 'num_remote_blocks': 4, 'local_block_ids_sample': [1, 2]} --- <details> <summary> Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist </summary> - [x] The purpose of the PR, such as "Fix some issue (link existing issues this PR will resolve)". - [x] The test plan, such as providing test command. - [x] The test results, such as pasting the results comparison before and after, or e2e results - [ ] (Optional) The necessary documentation update, such as updating `supported_models.md` and `examples` for a new model. </details>
